claims.text: Post-processing heat or thermomechanical treatments modify the grain-boundary network in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Post-processing heat or thermomechanical treatments modify precipitate distributions in multiprincipal-element alloys.
The treatment-induced grain-boundary and precipitate modifications favor formation of a contiguous, stable oxide scale.
The modified microstructure reduces fast oxygen-diffusion paths.
The modified microstructure enhances adhesion of protective oxides.
Reduced oxygen ingress and improved oxide adhesion govern oxidation resistance and material integrity at high temperature.
The as-processed alloy has a non-optimized grain-boundary network and oxide-scale structure.
Modified grain-boundary character and precipitate distributions promote a well-adhered, uniform protective oxide scale.
A more homogeneous and adherent oxide limits further oxidation.
A more homogeneous and adherent oxide reduces spallation during thermal cycling.
Targeted treatment will produce slower oxidation rates than no or minimal post-processing under identical exposure conditions.
Targeted treatment will produce thinner and more uniform oxide scales than the untreated baseline.
Targeted treatment will produce oxide scales with greater adhesion than the untreated baseline.
Targeted treatment will preserve mechanical integrity better than the untreated baseline after high-temperature oxidation.
The proposed treatment benefit should hold at approximately 700–900°C when exposure does not induce overriding phase transformations.
Outside the proposed temperature and phase-stability conditions, the treatment effect may weaken or interact with other factors.
